newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Stora sees signs of European recovey.
newsitem.headline: Stora sees signs of European recovey.

text.p: Swedish forestry group Stora said on Thursday it saw signs of a recovery in European markets as the strong dollar had a positive effect.
Stora reported a 54 percent fall in first quarter profit after financial items to 560 million crowns, saying lower prices had a negative impact of 1.7 billion crowns.
But currency fluctuations improved earnings by 100 million crowns.
"The strong economic trend in the U.S. continues. In Europe there are signs of a recovery, with the strong USD exchange rate having a positive effect," the company said in a statement of results.
It said that the market for sawn timber, paper and board improved compared with the same period in 1996, part of which was due to customer inventory reductions in 1996.
It said the order backlog for most of its products was from three to five weeks.
The group said that deliveries of pulp, paper and board rose by nine percent to 1.64 million tonnes with delivery levels unchanged versus the final quarter of last year.
It said the average sales prices for paper and board products were a lot lower, down by 17 percent compared with the first quarter of 1996 and down two percent versus Q4 1996.
Prices for printing papers and packaging were about eight percent lower while board and fine paper prices rose slightly. The price trend for sawn timber was also positive, it added.
The group said it generated earnings in the interest rate and currency markets and in share-related instruments.

The group said that a slump in earnings at the printing papers business was due to reduced prices while earnings growth in the technical papers area was due to price rises in late 1996 and February 1997.
Fine papers saw income rise due to higher volumes and improved margins while board and packaging paper saw a fall in earnings due to test runs of new products and trimming in of new machines.
In the base products division, power profits rose, partly due to increased hydropower production while forest also gained due to lower felling costs and a rise in volumes.
The pulp business saw a larger loss, hit by persistently high inventory levels.
